newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDA to decide soon on assuring juice safety.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDA to decide soon on assuring juice safety.

text.p: Regulators will decide by early 1997 whether additional steps are needed to assure juices are safe to drink, a high-ranking U.S. Food and Drug Administration official said Monday.
"The agency will decide if any future regulatory initiatives are necessary" in the first quarter of 1997, said Fred Shank, head of FDA's Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition.
Shank said FDA would look at a range of steps including new labeling rules, a public education campaign and directions to processors to adopt methods that prevent contamination of juices.
FDA called a two-day hearing on fresh juice manufacturing in the wake of an outbreak of E. coli O157:H7, a pathogen, in unpastuerized apple juice several weeks ago in the West. One child died.
The meeting was to conclude Tuesday with discussion of new technology to assure safety and a discussion of "What advice should be given to consumers?"
An industry group, the National Food Processors Association, said juices or juice ingredients should be pastuerized or given some other form of treatment as a disease prevention step.

Caroline Smith DeWaal, of the consumer group Center for Science in the Public Interest, said FDA should require labels so consumers would know if a product was pastuerized. She also called for an education campaign about fresh and pastuerized juices. DeWaal said FDA also should consider requiring all firms to adopt so-called HACCP -- Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point -- practices.
HACCP ensures food safety by focusing on steps where contamination might occur.
"Now, we go from outbreak to outbreak," DeWaal said.
During Monday's session, speakers cited technologies, such as high-pressure treatment, pulse light, irradiation and electromagnetic fields that might complement pastuerization as a treatment.
At present, FDA does not allow pastuerized products to be sold as "fresh."
Some juice makers regard mandatory pastuerization as an expensive and possibly unnecessary precaution if other treatments prove effective.
FDA has required HACCP adoption in industries such as seafood as a way to assure food safety.
